prompt:
Scene:
Create a square atlas plate for a speculative world, combining map readability, legend structure, and environmental storytelling in one disciplined layout. The image can use parchment, print, vellum, or technical drafting textures, but the map itself must remain crisp and intentionally organized. Use borders, inset frames, line weights, and abstract symbols as hierarchy tools rather than decoration. Build a continent map with terrain bands, faction overlays, route lines, and structured legend compartments around the edges of the square.

Subject:
Center the image on one coherent worldbuilding map system: coasts, terrain bands, faction territories, routes, hazard zones, inset diagrams, and legend compartments should all belong to the same cartographic language. The map should feel ready for a worldbook, poster, or campaign deck, not like a generic fantasy prop. Establish the reference map language through one major coastline, several political regions, controlled route density, and a few inset environmental diagrams.

Important details:
Maintain the authority of cartography without readable text. Symbol sets, route patterns, scale bars, seals, and legend blocks may appear as abstract information shapes. The image should reward close inspection through landform logic, political structure, and clear information hierarchy. The anchor plate should lock the line weight, symbol family, palette rules, and inset placement for the rest of the series. Resolve the anchor rules that later reference-dependent variants must inherit, especially the coastline shape language, legend placement, faction color hierarchy, and route symbol grammar.

Use case:
Atlas Set series study 1/4, designed as a reusable core-system image for this topic.

Constraints:
No readable text, no watermark, no logos, preserve exact 1:1 aspect ratio, no modern satellite UI, no readable text, no generic fantasy parchment stains overwhelming the map, no compass-logo branding, no decorative ship illustration clutter.
